For thousands of years, one of the most famous monuments on Earth was slowly disappearing beneath the desert.

The Great Sphinx of Giza wasn’t always sitting in full view like it is today. At different points in history, shifting sand buried almost its entire body. Imagine standing in the Egyptian desert and seeing nothing but a gigantic human head emerging from the sand.

That was the Sphinx.

Ancient and mysterious, it had been sitting there since around 4,500 years ago, watching kingdoms rise and collapse around it. By the time modern explorers arrived, much of its enormous lion-shaped body had vanished beneath the desert floor.

Old photographs make the story even more unbelievable. They show the massive head staring out across the sand while the rest of the monument remained hidden, as if some enormous creature had been trapped underground.

Then the digging began.

Slowly, layer by layer, the sand was removed. What emerged was far larger and stranger than the view people had known for centuries: the full body of a gigantic lion with a human head, carved directly from the limestone beneath the shadow of the pyramids.

And that’s where the mystery begins.

Why was it built? Who was its face meant to represent? Why combine a human with a lion? And after thousands of years of excavation and research, why are there still so many questions surrounding it?

Its nose is gone. Its face is damaged. Its stone body is covered in scars left by time and weather.

Yet there is something unsettling about the Sphinx.

It has no expression of fear. No sign of weakness. It simply sits there, staring silently towards the horizon.

More than 4,500 years have passed.

Pharaohs are gone. Their cities have disappeared. The people who built this enormous monument turned to dust thousands of years ago.

But the Sphinx is still there.

Still staring.

And perhaps still hiding secrets beneath the sands of Egypt.

Tony Pollard

Pollard is coming off a monster Week 7 game, and a solid game before that (76 rush yards), but I think things come crashing back down to earth in Week 8 for him.

Contrary to the norm for Pollard, he’s seen two neutral-to-positive game scripts over the last 2 weeks against two other bad teams (IND/CLE), which has allowed for 22 rushes per game. That seems almost certain to change here, as the Titans are +12.5 dogs against the Bengals in this one. This offense, as a reminder, is still quite horrid. They’re 31st in the NFL in total EPA, per @FantasyPtsData.

For the matchup, the Bengals rush defense has been relatively solid with the addition of Dexter Lawrence, sitting around league average in EPA/Rush, YPC, and explosive rush rate (despite a pretty tough schedule to start). They’ve been particularly good against runs to the outside (TEN runs outside at an above-average rate), allowing the 7th lowest YPC in the NFL and 6th lowest EPA/Rush there.

The Bengals have also been good defending runs out of 11 personnel, 10th best in YPC allowed. The Titans are frequently in 11 personnel, and run the ball out of it at the 2nd highest rate. 

I think the path is quite thin for Pollard here, in a script that should minimize rush volume.

Ja’Marr Chase

There’s a growing narrative around Ja’Marr Chase having not put up 100 yards yet this season, but I suspect that gets quickly put to rest in Week 8. In “squeaky wheel” fashion, I think we could see a ton of volume for Chase this weekend in a game where the Bengals will likely be able to win however they so choose. I’d imagine they'll try their best to feed arguably the NFL’s best receiver in this one.

The matchup is awesome for Chase, facing a Titans pass defense that’s 24th in EPA/DB and 27th in YPA allowed, despite one of the easiest schedules for a pass defense to date (have faced 7th worst passing offense on average by YPA). The Titans have been similarly weak on the perimeter (bottom 12 in YPG allowed).

In terms of coverage, the Titans run a ton of Cover 4 and Cover 6 with a top 3 and 6 rate, respectively. Chase has seen a massive boost against Cover 4 since the start of last year (0.28→0.33 TPRR, 2.21→3.37 YPRR), and particularly so in 2026 (0.25→0.33 TPRR, 1.92→3.32 YPRR). He’s also notably more efficient against Cover 6, jumping from 2.21→2.88 YPRR over the past year plus, and even more efficient on his very limited 2026 sample per @FantasyPtsData.

I think this is the theoretical get-right game for Chase, who has still been producing well despite not hitting triple-digit yardage this year (65 YPG, 8.4 targets per game).
